chem_ocra.16.0.summary: Organic chemistry focuses on compounds containing carbon atoms, which form the backbone of homologous series defined by specific functional groups. Alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, and carboxylic acids each possess unique chemical properties, general formulae, and bonding characteristics. Mastering these families, their structural representations, and naming conventions is essential for top grades in OCR GCSE Chemistry.

core.h: Introduction to Organic Chemistry and Hydrocarbons
core.p: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon can form four strong covalent bonds, allowing it to create long chains, rings, and complex branched structures. Hydrocarbons are compounds consisting exclusively of carbon and hydrogen atoms only.
bullets: Carbon forms four covalent bonds because it has four electrons in its outer shell.
Hydrocarbons contain only carbon (C) and hydrogen (H) atoms.
Organic molecules are represented using empirical, molecular, displayed, and structural formulae.

callouts.p: A compound containing hydrogen and carbon only.
Do not state that organic molecules contain carbon and water. They contain carbon and hydrogen.

core.p: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds that have the same general formula, similar chemical properties, and show a gradual trend in physical properties such as boiling point as molecular size increases.
bullets: All members of a homologous series share the same functional group.
Consecutive members differ by a CH2 structural unit.
As chain length increases, boiling points increase due to stronger intermolecular forces.
Chemical properties remain very similar because members share the same functional group.

callouts.p: A series of compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, in which each successive member differs by CH2.
Larger molecules have more intermolecular attractions to overcome, requiring more thermal energy and thus higher boiling points.

core.p: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms responsible for the typical chemical reactions of a molecule. Organic nomenclature follows strict IUPAC rules based on the longest carbon chain and the suffix of the functional group.
bullets: Prefixes depend on the number of carbons: Meth- (1), Eth- (2), Prop- (3), But- (4).
Alkanes end in '-ane' (no functional group, just single bonds).
Alkenes end in '-ene' (contain a carbon-carbon double bond).
Alcohols end in '-ol' (contain an -OH hydroxyl group).
Carboxylic acids end in '-oic acid' (contain a -COOH carboxyl group).

callouts.p: An atom or group of atoms that determines the chemical properties of a homologous series.

core.p: Alkanes are a homologous series of saturated hydrocarbons. They contain only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms and have the general formula CnH2n+2. Because all bonds are single sigma bonds, they are relatively unreactive except in combustion and substitution reactions.
bullets: General formula: CnH2n+2.
Saturated means they contain only single carbon-carbon bonds.
Methane, ethane, propane, and butane are the first four straight-chain alkanes.
They undergo combustion in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water (or carbon monoxide if oxygen is limited).

callouts.p: An organic compound containing only single carbon-carbon bonds (no double or triple bonds).
Always check your alkane formula: if n = 5, hydrogens = (2 x 5) + 2 = 12 (C5H12).

core.h: Alkenes: Unsaturated Hydrocarbons and Bromine Test
core.p: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C). Their general formula is CnH2n. The presence of the double bond makes them much more reactive than alkanes, undergoing addition reactions where the double bond opens up.
bullets: General formula: CnH2n.
Unsaturated means they contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
Functional group is the C=C double bond.
Test for unsaturation: Bromine water turns from orange-brown to colourless when mixed with an alkene.

callouts.p: An organic compound containing at least one carbon-carbon double (or triple) bond.
Alkenes decolorise orange bromine water instantly. Alkanes do not react with bromine water in the dark (remain orange).

core.p: Alcohols contain the hydroxyl functional group (-OH) attached to a hydrocarbon chain. Their general formula is CnH2n+1OH. They are important solvents and fuels, and ethanol is the alcohol found in alcoholic drinks.
bullets: General formula: CnH2n+1OH.
Functional group: -OH (hydroxyl group).
First four members: methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol.
Dissolve in water to form neutral solutions.
React with sodium metal to produce hydrogen gas and a metal alkoxide.
Can be oxidized by acidified potassium manganate(VII) or microbial action to form carboxylic acids.

callouts.p: The hydroxyl group (-OH).

core.p: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl functional group (-COOH). Their general formula is CnH2n+1COOH. They behave as weak acids in water, meaning they only partially dissociate to release hydrogen ions.
bullets: General formula: CnH2n+1COOH.
Functional group: -COOH (carboxyl group).
First four members: methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid, butanoic acid.
Dissolve in water to form acidic solutions (pH < 7).
React with carbonates to produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas (effervescence).
React with metals to produce a salt and hydrogen gas.
React with alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst to form esters.

callouts.p: The carboxyl group (-COOH).
Carboxylic acids are weak acids because their ionisation in water is partial (reversible reaction), unlike strong mineral acids like hydrochloric acid which ionise fully.

core.p: Comparing the general formulae, functional groups, and reactions of alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, and carboxylic acids highlights how small changes in molecular structure lead to vastly different chemical behaviors.
bullets: Alkanes: CnH2n+2, saturated, unreactive with bromine water.
Alkenes: CnH2n, unsaturated (C=C), decolourise bromine water.
Alcohols: CnH2n+1OH, hydroxyl group (-OH), neutral pH.
Carboxylic acids: CnH2n+1COOH, carboxyl group (-COOH), weak acid pH 3-5.

callouts.p: Use bromine water to separate alkanes from alkenes, and sodium carbonate to separate carboxylic acids from alcohols.

analogy.p: Imagine a homologous series as a set of spanners of different sizes (carbon chain lengths). Every spanner in the set has the exact same gripping head (functional group), meaning they all do the same basic job (chemical reactions), just on bolts of different sizes. Where this breaks down is that physical properties like weight and grip handling change smoothly with size, whereas chemical reactivity for functional groups remains largely identical.

terms.d: The study of carbon compounds.
A compound consisting of hydrogen and carbon only.
A family of compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, differing by CH2.
An atom or group of atoms responsible for the typical chemical reactions of a molecule.
A saturated hydrocarbon with the general formula CnH2n+2.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing a C=C double bond with the general formula CnH2n.
An organic compound containing the -OH hydroxyl functional group.
An organic compound containing the -COOH carboxyl functional group.
Containing only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms.
Containing at least one carbon-carbon double or triple bond.
An algebraic formula that can describe any member of a homologous series.
An acid that only partially ionises in aqueous solution.

mistakes.w: Saying alkanes have a C-C double bond.
mistakes.r: Alkanes are saturated and contain only single carbon-carbon bonds.

mistakes.w: Writing the alcohol functional group as just H.
mistakes.r: The alcohol functional group is -OH (hydroxyl).

mistakes.w: Stating that carboxylic acids are strong acids.
mistakes.r: Carboxylic acids are weak acids because they only partially dissociate in water.

mistakes.w: Forgetting that alkenes decolourise bromine water.
mistakes.r: Alkenes turn bromine water from orange-brown to colourless; alkanes leave it orange.

mistakes.w: Writing the general formula of alkenes as CnH2n+2.
mistakes.r: CnH2n+2 is for alkanes; alkenes are CnH2n.

mistakes.w: Stating hydrocarbons contain oxygen.
mistakes.r: Hydrocarbons contain strictly carbon and hydrogen only.

mistakes.w: Calling -COOH the carbonyl group.
mistakes.r: -COOH is the carboxyl group; carbonyl refers to C=O.

exam.q: State the general formula for alkanes.
model: CnH2n+2
exam.tip: Must include correct subscript positioning.

exam.q: Explain why propene is described as an unsaturated hydrocarbon.
model: It contains carbon and hydrogen only (hydrocarbon)
It contains a carbon-carbon double bond (unsaturated)
exam.tip: Award one mark for each definition component.

exam.q: Describe what is observed when bromine water is added to butane and to butene.
model: Butane is an alkane / saturated
Bromine water remains orange-brown with butane
Butene is an alkene / unsaturated
Bromine water turns colourless with butene
exam.tip: Make sure to contrast both substances clearly.

exam.q: Give the name of the functional group found in all alcohols.
model: Hydroxyl (group) / -OH
exam.tip: Do not just write OH without the minus sign or name.

exam.q: Explain why ethanoic acid is classified as a weak acid.
model: It partially ionises in water
It produces a lower concentration of hydrogen ions than a strong acid of the same concentration
exam.tip: Key phrase is 'partially ionises'.

exam.q: Draw the displayed formula of ethene.
model: Correct C=C double bond with two hydrogens attached to each carbon atom
exam.tip: All bonds must connect properly to carbon atoms.

exam.q: Name the homologous series that has the general formula CnH2n.
model: Alkenes
exam.tip: Check formula carefully against alkanes and alkenes.

exam.q: Describe the chemical test to show that a solution contains a carboxylic acid using sodium carbonate.
model: Add sodium carbonate to the solution
Effervescence / fizzing is observed
Gas turns limewater milky (confirming carbon dioxide)
exam.tip: Mention both the observation and the gas test for full marks.

worked.q: Determine the molecular formula of an alkane containing 8 carbon atoms.
steps: Identify the homologous series: Alkane.
Recall the general formula for alkanes: CnH2n+2.
Substitute n = 8 into the general formula: C8H((2x8)+2).
Calculate hydrogen atoms: (2 x 8) + 2 = 18.

worked.q: Calculate the number of hydrogen atoms in an alkene with 6 carbon atoms.
steps: Identify the homologous series: Alkene.
Recall the general formula for alkenes: CnH2n.
Substitute n = 6 into the general formula: C6H(2x6).
Calculate hydrogen atoms: 2 x 6 = 12.

chem_ocra.16.2.summary: Addition polymerisation is a reaction where many small unsaturated alkene molecules, known as monomers, join together under high pressure and with a catalyst to form a single giant saturated molecule called a polymer. The carbon-carbon double bond in the alkene breaks open, allowing each monomer to bond to two neighbours, leaving a repeating unit with single bonds only. Because the resulting plastics contain strong carbon-carbon single covalent bonds, they are chemically inert and non-biodegradable, causing major environmental waste challenges.

core.p: Addition polymerisation is the specific chemical process by which thousands of small, unsaturated molecules called monomers join together to form one very large molecule called a polymer. No other product is formed in this reaction; the atom economy is exactly 100%.
bullets: Monomers must contain a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C), making them unsaturated alkenes.
The polymer backbone consists entirely of single covalent bonds between carbon atoms.
The reaction requires high pressure, a suitable catalyst, and sometimes heat.
The name of the polymer is derived from the monomer by simply adding 'poly-' in front, or enclosing the monomer name in brackets.

callouts.p: A reaction in which many small unsaturated monomers join together using addition reactions to form a single long-chain polymer as the only product.
Because all the atoms in the monomer molecules are utilised to form the polymer chain, addition polymerisation has a 100% atom economy.

core.h: Monomers and Polymers: Ethene to Poly(ethene)
core.p: Ethene is the simplest alkene monomer. When subjected to polymerisation conditions, the double bond between the two carbon atoms breaks, allowing the carbon atoms to link up into long chains of poly(ethene), commonly known as polythene.
bullets: Monomer formula: C2H4 (H2C=CH2).
Polymer formula: (C2H4)n or [-CH2-CH2-]n.
Poly(ethene) is flexible, electrical insulator, and cheap; used for plastic bags and bottles.
Low density poly(ethene) (LDPE) is formed at high pressure with trace oxygen; high density (HDPE) uses a Ziegler-Natta catalyst at lower pressure.

callouts.p: Always ensure the polymer repeating unit has single bonds and bonds extending outside the square brackets crossing the brackets.

core.h: Drawing Repeating Units and Polymer Chains
core.p: OCR exam questions frequently require you to deduce the polymer from a given monomer, or vice versa. Mastering the structural representation using square brackets and the subscript 'n' is essential for full marks.
bullets: Step 1: Draw the monomer with its C=C double bond horizontal.
Step 2: Change the C=C double bond into a C-C single bond.
Step 3: Draw bonds extending from each carbon atom through the left and right square brackets.
Step 4: Place the subscript 'n' outside the bottom right of the square bracket.

callouts.p: Never leave a double bond inside the repeating unit of the polymer! All polymer backbones from addition reactions are fully saturated.

core.p: If you are given a section of a polymer chain or its repeating unit, you must be able to work backwards to identify the original alkene monomer.
bullets: Step 1: Locate the repeating unit inside the square brackets or identify the repeating two-carbon pattern in a long chain.
Step 2: Write down the two carbon atoms with their attached groups as a single monomer unit.
Step 3: Change the single bond between the two carbon atoms into a double bond (C=C).
Step 4: Remove the square brackets, extension bonds, and the subscript 'n'.

callouts.p: The carbon backbone of the repeating unit directly corresponds to the two carbon atoms of the original alkene monomer.

core.p: Poly(chloroethene), commonly known as PVC (polyvinyl chloride), is produced by the addition polymerisation of chloroethene (vinyl chloride) monomers.
bullets: Monomer: CH2=CHCl (chloroethene), where one hydrogen atom on ethene is replaced by a chlorine atom.
Polymer formula: [-CH2-CHCl-]n.
Properties: Rigid, durable, waterproof, and an electrical insulator.
Uses: Window frames, water pipes, cable insulation, and vinyl flooring.

callouts.p: Due to polar C-Cl bonds and strong intermolecular forces, PVC is harder and more rigid than pure poly(ethene).

core.p: Poly(propene) (polypropylene) is formed when propene monomers undergo addition polymerisation. Propene has a methyl group (-CH3) attached to one of the carbons.
bullets: Monomer: CH3-CH=CH2 (propene).
Polymer repeating unit: [-CH(CH3)-CH2-]n with side chains extending from the backbone.
Properties: Tough, strong, resists fatigue and chemical corrosion.
Uses: Ropes, crates, carpets, and microwave containers.

core.p: Poly(tetrafluoroethene), known commercially as Teflon or PTFE, is made by polymerising tetrafluoroethene, where all four hydrogen atoms of ethene are replaced by fluorine atoms.
bullets: Monomer: CF2=CF2 (tetrafluoroethene).
Polymer formula: [-CF2-CF2-]n.
Properties: Extremely unreactive, exceptionally low friction, heat resistant.
Uses: Non-stick coating for frying pans, Gore-Tex breathable fabrics, and electrical tape.

callouts.p: The carbon-fluorine bond is one of the strongest in organic chemistry, giving PTFE its remarkable thermal and chemical stability.

core.p: The physical and chemical properties of addition polymers are directly determined by their molecular structure and the intermolecular forces acting between the long polymer chains.
bullets: Chains are held together by intermolecular forces (London dispersion forces).
Longer chains have more points of contact, stronger intermolecular forces, and higher melting points.
Because their carbon backbones consist solely of strong C-C and C-H single bonds, they are unreactive towards most acids and alkalis.
They do not conduct electricity because there are no free-moving charged particles or delocalised electrons.

core.p: A major societal issue associated with addition polymers is their disposal. Because their saturated carbon backbones are extremely strong and chemically stable, microorganisms cannot break them down.
bullets: Addition polymers are **non-biodegradable**, meaning they persist in landfill sites for hundreds of years.
Discarded plastics pollute oceans, harming marine life through entanglement and ingestion.
Incinerating plastics destroys them and releases thermal energy, but produces toxic gases like hydrogen chloride (from PVC) and carbon dioxide, contributing to global warming.
Recycling is difficult because different polymers must be sorted carefully before melting and remoulding, as mixed plastics yield poor-quality materials.

callouts.p: Do not state that polymers burn to produce toxic gases without specifying which polymer (e.g., PVC releases HCl gas).

core.p: To gain top marks at GCSE, you must be able to distinguish between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation (covered in C6.2e).
bullets: Addition polymerisation uses one monomer type with a C=C double bond; condensation polymerisation often uses two different monomer types with two functional groups each.
Addition polymerisation produces only one product (the polymer); condensation polymerisation produces a polymer plus a small molecule like water (H2O) or HCl.
Addition polymerisation has 100% atom economy; condensation polymerisation has lower atom economy.

analogy.p: Imagine a box of open paperclips where each clip has a special clasp (the double bond). When you apply pressure and shake the box, the clasps pop open and hook onto the neighbouring clips, linking together into a long metal chain. Each individual clip was a monomer, and the resulting chain is the polymer. Where the analogy breaks down: real alkene monomers require a specific chemical catalyst and precise industrial pressure, and the monomers are converted into saturated single-bonded carbon units rather than mechanical clasps.

terms.d: A small, reactive molecule, usually containing a C=C double bond, that can join with other molecules to form a polymer.
A large molecule formed by joining many thousands of monomer molecules together in a long chain.
A reaction where many unsaturated monomers join together to form a polymer as the sole product.
The shortest section of a polymer chain which, if repeated many times, would yield the entire polymer molecule.
Describes an organic compound containing at least one carbon-carbon double or triple bond.
Describes an organic compound containing only carbon-carbon single bonds.
An addition polymer produced from ethene monomers, used widely for plastic bags and containers.
Poly(chloroethene), a rigid polymer produced from chloroethene used for pipes and window frames.
Poly(tetrafluoroethene), a heat-resistant, non-stick polymer used for pan coatings.
Unable to be broken down by microorganisms or natural biological processes.
A measure of the proportion of starting materials that end up as useful products in a chemical reaction.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself.

mistakes.w: Leaving a double bond inside the polymer repeating unit.
mistakes.r: All addition polymers have saturated carbon backbones with C-C single bonds only.

mistakes.w: Stating that addition polymerisation produces water as a byproduct.
mistakes.r: Addition polymerisation has 100% atom economy and produces the polymer ONLY. Water is produced in condensation polymerisation.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the square brackets and the subscript 'n' when drawing polymers.
mistakes.r: Square brackets intersecting the bonds and the subscript 'n' outside are strictly required by OCR mark schemes.

mistakes.w: Writing the monomer formula inside the polymer brackets without changing the double bond.
mistakes.r: The double bond must be shown as a single bond inside the brackets with bonds extending out the sides.

mistakes.w: Describing plastics as being biodegradable.
mistakes.r: Addition polymers are non-biodegradable because strong C-C and C-H bonds resist bacterial attack.

mistakes.w: Saying that ethene is a polymer.
mistakes.r: Ethene is the monomer; poly(ethene) is the polymer.

exam.q: Define the term 'monomer' in the context of addition polymerisation.
model: A small molecule / alkene
With a carbon-carbon double bond that joins to form a polymer
exam.tip: Mention both that it is a small molecule and that it contains a double bond.

exam.q: Explain why addition polymerisation has an atom economy of 100%.
model: All the atoms in the monomer molecules
Are used to form the polymer chain with no other products formed
exam.tip: State clearly that no other byproduct is created.

exam.q: Draw the repeating unit of poly(ethene).
model: Correct carbon-carbon single bond backbone with two hydrogens on each carbon
Square brackets enclosing the unit with bonds extending outside and subscript 'n'
exam.tip: Ensure bonds pass cleanly through the square brackets.

exam.q: The monomer propene has the formula CH3CH=CH2. Draw the repeating unit of poly(propene).
model: Carbon backbone with single bonds, CH3 attached to one carbon
Square brackets with extension bonds and subscript n
exam.tip: Place the methyl group (-CH3) on one of the backbone carbons as a side branch.

exam.q: Name the polymer formed from chloroethene and give one of its uses.
model: Poly(chloroethene) / PVC
Water pipes / window frames / cable insulation
exam.tip: Both names (poly(chloroethene) or PVC) are accepted by OCR.

exam.q: Explain why addition polymers are non-biodegradable.
model: They have strong carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen single covalent bonds
Which cannot be broken down by microorganisms or enzymes
exam.tip: Focus on bond strength and lack of biological attack.

exam.q: A polymer has the repeating unit [-CF2-CF2-]n. Deduce the formula of the monomer.
model: CF2=CF2
exam.tip: Simply change the single bond back into a double bond.

exam.q: Discuss the environmental problems caused by the disposal of addition polymers.
model: Non-biodegradable so persist in landfill sites for a long time
Disposal in oceans harms marine life through entanglement or ingestion
Incineration releases carbon dioxide (contributing to global warming)
Incineration of certain polymers (like PVC) can release toxic hydrogen chloride gas
exam.tip: Give at least two distinct environmental impacts with explanations for full marks.

exam.q: Compare addition polymerisation with condensation polymerisation in terms of products formed.
model: Addition polymerisation produces only the polymer
Condensation polymerisation produces a polymer and a small molecule such as water
exam.tip: Mention water or small molecules for the condensation mark.

worked.q: Deduce the structure of the monomer that forms the polymer with the repeating unit [-CH(CH3)-CH2-]n.
steps: Identify the repeating unit inside the brackets: [-CH(CH3)-CH2-].
Write out the two central carbon atoms connected by a single bond.
Attach the relevant groups: one carbon has a hydrogen and a methyl group (-CH3), the other carbon has two hydrogens.
Change the single bond between the two carbon atoms into a double bond (C=C) to form the monomer.

worked.q: A company produces 560 tonnes of poly(ethene) from ethene. Calculate the mass of ethene monomer required, assuming a 100% percentage yield.
steps: Recall that addition polymerisation has 100% atom economy.
Mass of polymer produced = Mass of monomer required.
Substitute the given mass: 560 tonnes of polymer requires 560 tonnes of monomer.

chem_ocra.16.1.summary: This section covers the crucial chemical reactions of organic compounds specific to the OCR GCSE Chemistry triple-tier specification: complete and incomplete combustion, addition reactions of alkenes, and oxidation of alcohols to carboxylic acids. Mastering these reactions requires understanding functional groups, balancing balanced symbol equations, and recognising the specific colour changes used in tests such as bromine water.

core.p: Combustion is the scientific term for burning. When organic compounds containing carbon and hydrogen (such as alkanes, alkenes, or alcohols) burn in an excess of oxygen, complete combustion takes place, producing carbon dioxide and water.
bullets: Reactants are the organic fuel and excess oxygen gas.
Products are strictly carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O).
Energy is released in an exothermic reaction.
General equation for an alkane: CnH(2n+2) + ((3n+1)/2)O2 -> nCO2 + (n+1)H2O.
Example for methane: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O.

callouts.p: Combustion reactions transfer thermal energy to the surroundings, making them strongly exothermic.

core.p: When organic compounds burn in a limited supply of oxygen, incomplete combustion occurs. This reaction fails to oxidise all the carbon atoms completely, leading to hazardous by-products.
bullets: Produces carbon monoxide (CO), a toxic, odourless, colourless gas.
Produces unburnt carbon particulates (soot, C), which dirty surfaces and cause global dimming.
Still produces water vapour (H2O).
Associated with a smoky, yellow, luminous flame rather than a clean blue flame.
Example for ethane: 2C2H6 + 5O2 -> 4CO + 6H2O.

callouts.p: Carbon monoxide binds irreversibly to haemoglobin in red blood cells, starving the body of oxygen and causing death.

core.p: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C). This double bond is a region of high electron density and is reactive, making alkenes undergo addition reactions where two reactant molecules combine to form a single product.
bullets: The carbon-carbon double bond opens up during an addition reaction.
One single bond is replaced by two new single sigma bonds.
No other products are formed (atom economy is 100%).
Alkenes react with hydrogen, halogens, and steam.
Alkanes cannot undergo addition reactions because they are saturated.

callouts.p: A reaction in which two or more molecules combine to form a larger molecule with no other products.

core.p: Hydrogenation is the addition of hydrogen gas (H2) across the carbon-carbon double bond of an alkene to produce a saturated alkane.
bullets: Requires a nickel catalyst and high temperatures (approx 150°C - 200°C).
Ethene + Hydrogen -> Ethane (C2H4 + H2 -> C2H6).
Used commercially in the food industry to convert liquid vegetable oils into solid fats like margarine.
The product has higher melting points than the starting material due to tighter molecular packing.

callouts.p: Nickel is essential to lower the activation energy for the hydrogenation reaction.

core.p: Alkenes react readily with halogens (such as bromine, chlorine, or iodine) at room temperature without requiring any catalyst. Bromine water is the standard chemical test used to distinguish alkenes from alkanes.
bullets: Ethene + Bromine -> 1,2-dibromoethane (C2H4 + Br2 -> C2H4Br2).
Colour change: Bromine water turns from bright orange/brown to colourless when mixed with an alkene.
Alkanes do not react with bromine water at room temperature, so the solution remains orange.
The rapidity of the colour change indicates unsaturation (the presence of a C=C bond).

callouts.p: Always state that bromine water turns 'colourless', not 'clear'. Clear means transparent like water; colourless means having no colour.

core.p: Alkenes react with steam (water vapour) in an addition reaction known as hydration to produce alcohols. This is an industrial process used to manufacture ethanol.
bullets: Conditions: High temperature (approx 300°C), high pressure (approx 60-70 atmospheres), and a phosphoric acid (H3PO4) catalyst.
Ethene + Steam -> Ethanol (C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH).
The reaction is reversible; unreacted ethene and steam are recycled through the reaction chamber.
Provides a high yield of pure ethanol but relies on crude oil fractions as the source of ethene.

callouts.p: Remember the three industrial requirements: 300°C, 60 atm, and phosphoric acid catalyst.

core.p: Alcohols contain the hydroxyl functional group (-OH). When treated with suitable oxidising agents, primary alcohols can be oxidised to form carboxylic acids containing the carboxyl group (-COOH).
bullets: The oxidising agent commonly used in the laboratory is acidified potassium manganate(VII) or acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) changes colour from orange to green during the reaction.
Oxidation involves the gain of oxygen atoms and/or loss of hydrogen atoms.
Ethanol + [O] -> Ethanoic acid + Water (CH3CH2OH + 2[O] -> CH3COOH + H2O).

callouts.p: A substance that accepts electrons or adds oxygen to another substance, getting reduced in the process.

core.p: In the laboratory, oxidising ethanol to ethanoic acid is carried out using a heated mixture of ethanol and acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux to prevent volatile organic vapours from escaping.
bullets: Reflux apparatus involves heating a reaction mixture with a vertical Liebig condenser attached, so vapours condense and drop back into the flask.
Colour changes from orange (Cr2O7 2-) to green (Cr3+).
Carboxylic acids produced are weak acids that partially dissociate in water.
They react with carbonates to produce carbon dioxide gas, providing a test to distinguish them from alcohols.

callouts.p: Carboxylic acids react with sodium carbonate to fizz (release CO2). Alcohols do not react with carbonates.

core.p: Alcohols can also be oxidised by microbial action, which is how wine turns to vinegar when left exposed to air over time.
bullets: Acetobacter bacteria in the air use atmospheric oxygen to oxidise ethanol in wine to ethanoic acid.
This is a slow biological oxidation process.
Requires oxygen and warmth for microbial activity.
Results in the sour taste characteristic of vinegar.

callouts.p: Microbial oxidation uses bacteria and atmospheric oxygen rather than chemical oxidising agents like potassium dichromate.

core.h: 10. Comparing Combustion Properties Across Homologous Series
core.p: Different homologous series undergo combustion, but the ratio of carbon to hydrogen affects the appearance of their flames and the energy released per mole.
bullets: Alkanes with longer chains have higher percentages of carbon, leading to sootier flames during combustion.
Alcohols contain oxygen within their molecular structure, so they burn with cleaner flames than alkanes of equivalent chain length.
All combustion reactions of organic compounds are exothermic because new, stable bonds in CO2 and H2O release more energy than is required to break bonds in the reactants.
Enthalpy changes scale with the number of carbon dioxide molecules formed per mole of fuel.

core.p: Addition reactions are characteristic of unsaturated molecules. Every addition reaction involves breaking the pi component of the C=C double bond and forming two new single bonds.
bullets: Hydrogen + Alkene -> Alkane (Ni catalyst, 150°C).
Halogen + Alkene -> Dihaloalkane (Room temp, no catalyst, decolourises bromine water).
Steam + Alkene -> Alcohol (H3PO4 catalyst, 300°C, 60 atm).
All addition reactions have 100% atom economy because all reactant atoms are incorporated into the single target product.

callouts.p: Addition reactions are environmentally green because there are no waste by-products formed.

analogy.t: The Double Bond as a Handshake
analogy.p: Think of a carbon-carbon double bond as two people holding hands tightly with both hands (a double grip). When an addition reaction happens, they drop one hand grip and use those newly freed hands to shake hands with incoming new friends (like hydrogen or bromine atoms). In contrast, alkanes are like people standing side-by-side with their hands in their pockets (saturated), unable to grab anything new without letting go of an existing bond first. Where the analogy breaks down is that chemical bonds are electrostatic forces between nuclei and shared electron pairs, not literal human hands.

terms.d: The high-temperature exothermic reaction of a substance with oxygen.
Combustion in excess oxygen producing only carbon dioxide and water.
Combustion in limited oxygen producing carbon monoxide, soot, and water.
A reaction where two or more molecules combine to form a single product with 100% atom economy.
The addition of hydrogen across a C=C double bond to form an alkane, requiring a nickel catalyst.
The addition of a halogen across a C=C double bond, used as a test for unsaturation.
The addition of steam across a C=C double bond to form an alcohol, using a phosphoric acid catalyst.
The addition of oxygen to a substance, or loss of hydrogen/electrons.
A substance that brings about oxidation by transferring oxygen or accepting electrons.
Boiling a liquid and condensing the vapour continuously to prevent loss of volatile organic compounds.
Containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C).
Containing only single carbon-carbon bonds (C-C).

mistakes.w: Saying bromine water turns clear when added to an alkene.
mistakes.r: Bromine water turns colourless. Clear means transparent, whereas the solution remains transparent after the reaction, just without its orange colour.

mistakes.w: Writing that alkanes undergo addition reactions.
mistakes.r: Alkanes are saturated and only undergo substitution reactions, whereas alkenes undergo addition reactions due to their C=C double bond.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the catalyst for hydration of ethene.
mistakes.r: Must specify phosphoric acid (H3PO4), alongside 300°C and 60 atmospheres.

mistakes.w: Stating complete combustion produces carbon monoxide.
mistakes.r: Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water only. Carbon monoxide is a product of incomplete combustion.

mistakes.w: Omitting state symbols in organic combustion equations.
mistakes.r: Examiners frequently penalise missing or incorrect state symbols (g, l, s, aq) in specified symbol equations.

mistakes.w: Confusing hydrogenation with hydration.
mistakes.r: Hydrogenation adds H2 to make an alkane; hydration adds H2O (steam) to make an alcohol.

mistakes.w: Stating potassium dichromate turns clear.
mistakes.r: Acidified potassium dichromate changes from orange to green upon reduction by an alcohol.

exam.q: State the colour change observed when bromine water is added to ethene gas.
model: Orange / brown (1)
To colourless (1)
exam.tip: Never write 'clear'. Both marks depend on precise colour terminology.

exam.q: Explain why alkenes can undergo addition reactions, whereas alkanes cannot.
model: Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C) / are unsaturated (1)
Alkanes only contain single carbon-carbon bonds / are saturated (1)
exam.tip: Link the presence of the double bond directly to the ability to open up and form addition products.

exam.q: Write a balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of propane (C3H8).
model: Correct balancing and state symbols (1)
exam.tip: Balance carbons first, hydrogens second, and oxygen last.

exam.q: Describe the conditions required for the industrial hydration of ethene to produce ethanol.
model: Temperature of about 300°C (1)
Pressure of about 60 to 70 atmospheres (1)
Phosphoric acid catalyst (1)
exam.tip: All three conditions must be learned precisely as stated in the specification.

exam.q: Explain the hazard associated with the incomplete combustion of fuels in household heaters.
model: Produces carbon monoxide (1)
Which binds to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport in the blood (1)
exam.tip: State both the toxic product and its biological mode of action for full credit.

exam.q: Name the functional group formed when ethanol is oxidised with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
model: Carboxyl group / -COOH (1)
exam.tip: Give the name or formula of the functional group as requested.

exam.q: Describe how you could chemically distinguish between an alkane and an alkene.
model: Add bromine water to both liquids (1)
Alkane: bromine water remains orange (1)
Alkene: bromine water turns colourless (1)
exam.tip: Always structure test questions by stating the reagent, the sample, and both distinct expected observations.

exam.q: Calculate the atom economy for the production of ethanol from ethene and steam.
model: Reactants mass = 28 + 18 = 46 g/mol; Product mass = 46 g/mol (1)
exam.tip: Addition reactions always have 100% atom economy because there is only one product.

exam.q: Outline the colour change seen when an alcohol is oxidised using acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
model: From orange (1)
To green (1)
exam.tip: Memorise the exact colour transition for dichromate ions in organic oxidation.

worked.q: Write a balanced symbol equation for the hydrogenation of propene (C3H6) to form propane, including state symbols.
steps: Identify the reactant formula for propene: C3H6(g).
Identify the second reactant: hydrogen gas, H2(g).
Deduce the addition product: propane, C3H8(g).
Combine and check balancing: C3H6(g) + H2(g) -> C3H8(g).

worked.q: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 10.0 g of methane (CH4) undergoes complete combustion. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
steps: Write balanced equation: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O.
Calculate Mr of CH4 = 12 + (4 * 1) = 16.
Calculate Mr of CO2 = 12 + (2 * 16) = 44.
Moles of CH4 = mass / Mr = 10.0 / 16 = 0.625 mol.
Moles of CO2 produced = 0.625 mol (1:1 molar ratio).
Mass of CO2 = moles * Mr = 0.625 * 44 = 27.5 g.

chem_ocra.16.3.summary: Condensation polymerisation is a reaction where monomers with two functional groups join together to form a polymer chain, accompanied by the loss of a small molecule such as water or hydrogen chloride. Unlike addition polymerisation, which relies on the double bonds of alkenes, condensation polymerisation requires two different functional groups on each monomer or two complementary monomers reacting together. This process creates vital synthetic polymers like polyesters and polyamides, which include useful materials such as terylene and nylon.

core.h: Definition and Core Principles of Condensation Polymerisation
core.p: Condensation polymerisation is a type of step-growth polymerisation where monomers with two functional groups react to form long chains, releasing a small byproduct molecule with every bond formed.
bullets: Monomers require at least **two functional groups** per molecule to form a polymer chain.
A small molecule, most commonly **water (H2O)** or **hydrogen chloride (HCl)**, is eliminated during the reaction.
The backbone of the polymer chain contains functional ester or amide linkages.
Unlike addition polymerisation, no carbon-carbon double bonds are needed to open up.

callouts.p: A polymerisation reaction in which monomers join together to form a polymer with the elimination of a small molecule such as water.

fig.cap: Figure 1: General representation of condensation polymerisation showing monomers combining into a polymer chain and releasing water.

core.p: Examiners frequently test your ability to contrast addition and condensation polymerisation across various characteristics like monomer types, byproducts, and backbone structures.
bullets: Addition polymerisation uses one monomer type with a C=C double bond; condensation uses two functional groups.
Addition polymerisation produces only one product (the polymer); condensation produces a polymer plus a small molecule like water.
Addition polymers have an inert hydrocarbon backbone; condensation polymers have reactive ester or amide links.

callouts.p: Always check if a small molecule is lost when identifying polymerisation types.

core.p: Polyesters are formed through the reaction between a dicarboxylic acid monomer and a diol monomer, creating ester linkages along the polymer chain.
bullets: A **dicarboxylic acid** contains two -COOH groups (one at each end).
A **diol** contains two -OH alcohol groups (one at each end).
The -OH from the carboxylic acid and the -H from the alcohol combine to form a **water molecule (H2O)**.
The remaining parts join with an **ester link (-COO-)**.

callouts.p: The ester functional group is -COO- formed by the reaction of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.

fig.cap: Figure 2: Formation of a polyester link from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol, releasing water.

core.p: Terylene is a well-known synthetic polyester used extensively in the textile industry for manufacturing hard-wearing clothing and drinks bottles.
bullets: Monomers used: **benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid** and **ethane-1,2-diol**.
Chains are strong and crease-resistant, making them ideal for blended fabrics.
Can be spun into fibres or moulded into rigid plastic containers.

callouts.p: Learn the specific monomers for Terylene (PET) as exam questions often ask you to name or draw them.

core.p: Polyamides are formed when a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diamine, creating strong amide linkages (-CONH-) along the polymer backbone.
bullets: A **diamine** contains two amine groups (-NH2), one at each end of the molecule.
The -OH from the carboxylic acid and a -H from the amine combine to eliminate a **water molecule**.
The resulting bond is an **amide link (-CONH-)**.
Natural proteins are also polyamides formed from amino acids.

callouts.p: The amide functional group is -CONH- formed by the condensation reaction between a carboxylic acid and an amine.

core.p: Nylon is a synthetic polyamide discovered by DuPont scientists. It exhibits high tensile strength and elasticity.
bullets: Commonly made from **1,6-diaminohexane** and **hexanedioic acid** (Nylon-6,6).
Used to make ropes, parachutes, carpets, and mechanical gear components due to its low friction.
Can be drawn into fine, incredibly strong fibres.

callouts.p: The numbers 6,6 refer to the number of carbon atoms in each of the two monomers.

core.p: Amino acids are naturally occurring monomers that contain two different functional groups: an amine group (-NH2) and a carboxylic acid group (-COOH).
bullets: Because an amino acid has both an acid and an amine group, **a single monomer type** can undergo condensation polymerisation with itself.
The resulting polymer is called a **polypeptide** or protein.
Water is eliminated every time an amide (peptide) bond forms between two amino acid units.

callouts.p: Do not assume all condensation polymers need two different monomer molecules; amino acids polymerise on their own.

fig.cap: Figure 3: Amino acid polymerisation showing how a single amino acid with two different functional ends creates a polypeptide chain.

core.p: Condensation polymerisation is also responsible for key biological structures such as DNA and complex carbohydrates.
bullets: **DNA** is a polymer made from four different monomers called **nucleotides**, forming a double helix via condensation reactions.
**Starch and cellulose** are natural condensation polymers formed from sugar monomer units (like glucose), eliminating water.
These natural polymers are biodegradable, unlike many synthetic plastics.

callouts.p: Natural condensation polymers can be broken down by enzymes or hydrolysis, whereas addition polymers lack polar bonds and persist in the environment.

core.h: Disposal and Environmental Impact of Condensation Polymers
core.p: The presence of polar bonds in condensation polymers makes them susceptible to chemical attack, influencing how they degrade.
bullets: Ester and amide links can be broken down by **hydrolysis** (reaction with water) using acids, alkalis, or enzymes.
This means polyesters and polyamides are more readily biodegradable or recyclable than polyalkenes like poly(ethene).
Disposal methods include landfill, incineration (releasing energy), and chemical recycling back into monomers.

callouts.p: Remember that hydrolysis is the exact reverse of condensation polymerisation.

core.h: Interpreting Repeat Units for Condensation Polymers
core.p: Examiners will expect you to deduce the repeat unit of a condensation polymer from its monomers, or vice versa.
bullets: Identify the two functional groups on each monomer.
Remove -OH from the acid and -H from the alcohol/amine to form H2O.
Join the remaining fragments with the appropriate link (-COO- or -CONH-).
Enclose the repeat unit in square brackets with a subscript 'n' and show extension bonds outside the brackets.

callouts.p: Ensure extension bonds cross the square brackets of a repeat unit; leaving them inside loses marks.

analogy.p: Imagine condensation polymerisation like building a long train with two types of special Lego bricks: brick A has two plug ends, and brick B has two socket ends. When they click together, a tiny spacer pellet (representing water) falls out onto the floor. If you have thousands of bricks, you get a massive train and a pile of little spacer pellets. Where this breaks down: real monomers react continuously in solution at multiple active sites simultaneously rather than one by one from an engine.

mistakes.w: Saying addition polymers produce water as a byproduct.
mistakes.r: Addition polymers produce no byproducts; only condensation polymers release a small molecule.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the 'n' in front of H2O in balanced condensation equations.
mistakes.r: You must include '2n H2O' or 'n H2O' to balance moles of small molecules released.

mistakes.w: Drawing ester links as -COC- or -CCO-.
mistakes.r: The ester link must be written as -COO- or -CO-O- connecting the carbon to the oxygen.

mistakes.w: Stating that all condensation polymers require two different monomers.
mistakes.r: Amino acids have two different functional groups in one molecule and can polymerise on their own.

mistakes.w: Leaving the continuation bonds inside the square brackets of a repeat unit.
mistakes.r: Continuation bonds must pass through the square brackets to show the chain continues.

mistakes.w: Confusing amide and amine functional groups.
mistakes.r: Amine is -NH2; amide is the linkage -CONH- found within the polymer backbone.

exam.q: State what is meant by condensation polymerisation.
model: Reaction where monomers with two functional groups join
With the elimination of a small molecule such as water
exam.tip: Both marking points are essential for full credit.

exam.q: Explain one key difference between addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.
model: Addition polymerisation produces only the polymer
Condensation polymerisation also produces a small molecule such as water
exam.tip: You can also compare monomer types (alkenes vs two functional groups).

exam.q: Name the two types of functional groups that react together to form a polyester.
model: Carboxylic acid (or dicarboxylic acid)
Alcohol (or diol)
exam.tip: Make sure to specify 'di-' or plural if referring to the monomers.

exam.q: Name the linkage found in polyamides.
model: Amide link (or peptide link)
exam.tip: Write out the name clearly; formulas alone may not always suffice.

exam.q: Complete the missing word: Terylene is a polyester made from a dicarboxylic acid and a .......
model: diol
exam.tip: Know your specific examples for synthetic polymers.

exam.q: Explain why polyesters are generally biodegradable while polyethene is not.
model: Polyesters contain polar ester links in their backbone
These polar bonds can be attacked by water in hydrolysis or by enzymes
Polyethene has a non-polar carbon-carbon backbone which is inert to water
exam.tip: Link the presence of polar bonds to chemical attack.

exam.q: Draw the repeat unit of a polyester formed from HO-R-OH and HOOC-R'-COOH.
model: Correct ester link (-O-R-O-CO-R'-CO-) shown
Enclosed in square brackets with extension bonds passing through and subscript n
exam.tip: Check that your oxygen and carbonyl carbon atoms match the ester linkage.

exam.q: Describe how amino acids form proteins.
model: Amino acids contain both an amine group and a carboxylic acid group
The acid group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of another
A condensation reaction occurs, releasing water and forming an amide (peptide) link
exam.tip: Mention both functional groups on the single amino acid monomer.

exam.q: Calculate the mass of water produced when 0.5 moles of a dicarboxylic acid completely reacts with excess diol.
model: 1 mole of dicarboxylic acid and 1 mole of diol produce 2 moles of water per repeat unit, or 1 H2O per reacting end group (award based on stoichiometry)
Identify Mr of H2O = 18
Correct calculation leading to final mass
exam.tip: Read stoichiometry carefully regarding how many water molecules are lost per bond.

worked.q: Deduced Repeat Unit: What is the repeat unit of the polyester formed from ethane-1,2-diol (HO-CH2-CH2-OH) and hexanedioic acid (HOOC-(CH2)4-COOH)?
steps: Identify the diol part: -O-CH2-CH2-O-
Identify the dicarboxylic acid part: -CO-(CH2)4-CO-
Combine them with the ester link and enclose in brackets: [-O-CH2-CH2-O-CO-(CH2)4-CO-]n

worked.q: Byproduct calculation: How many moles of water are produced when 5 moles of a dicarboxylic acid react completely with 5 moles of a diol to form a long polyester chain?
steps: Each ester bond formed releases one molecule of water.

When n monomer pairs react to form a chain of length n, 2n water molecules are typically released at the chain ends, but for OCR calculations, consider that each reaction between an -OH and -COOH group produces 1 H2O.
For 5 moles of acid reacting with 5 moles of diol, 10 moles of water are produced.

chem_ocra.16.4.summary: Natural polymers are essential macromolecular substances found in living organisms, constructed from small repeating monomer units joined by chemical bonds. This topic covers carbohydrates, proteins, and DNA, exploring their monomer building blocks, structural diversity, and biological functions. Understanding these natural polymers bridges organic chemistry with biochemistry, highlighting how functional groups dictate polymer formation and properties.

core.p: Natural polymers are large molecules (macromolecules) built up by linking many smaller molecules called monomers together into long chains. Unlike synthetic addition polymers, natural polymers often possess specific biological functions determined by their precise chemical structure and sequence.
bullets: Macromolecules formed naturally by living organisms.
Consist of repeating units derived from small monomer molecules.
Crucial for life processes, structure, and genetic information storage.
Formed via condensation polymerisation reactions releasing small molecules like water.

callouts.p: A long-chain molecule made from repeating smaller monomer units that occurs naturally in living systems.
Small reactive molecules bond together repeatedly to create high relative molecular mass macromolecules.

core.p: Carbohydrates are organic compounds composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, generally with a hydrogen to oxygen ratio of 2:1. They range from small sugar monomers to giant complex polymers.
bullets: Monomers are simple sugars called monosaccharides (e.g., glucose, fructose).
Monosaccharides have formula C6H12O6 and contain hydroxyl (-OH) and carbonyl groups.
Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join with the elimination of water (e.g., sucrose, maltose).
Polysaccharides are large polymers formed by condensing many monosaccharide units together.

callouts.p: A simple sugar monomer that cannot be hydrolysed to give a simpler sugar.

core.p: Starch and cellulose are both important polysaccharides made entirely of glucose monomers, yet they exhibit vastly different physical properties due to how their monomer units are linked together.
bullets: Starch is used by plants as an energy storage molecule.
Cellulose provides rigid structural support in plant cell walls.
The difference arises from the spatial arrangement (stereochemistry) of bonds between glucose units.
Human enzymes can break down starch for energy, but cannot hydrolyse cellulose (dietary fibre).

callouts.p: Slight differences in monomer bonding drastically change whether a polymer is digestible energy or rigid structural fibre.
Always state that starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose monomers when asked.

core.p: Proteins are vital natural polymers that perform structural, enzymatic, and regulatory roles in living organisms. Their monomers are amino acids, which polymerise via condensation reactions.
bullets: Monomers are amino acids containing an amine group (-NH2) and a carboxylic acid group (-COOH).
There are 20 standard naturally occurring amino acids with different side chains (R groups).
Amino acids join together via peptide bonds, forming polypeptide chains.
Water is eliminated during the formation of each peptide bond (condensation polymerisation).

callouts.p: An organic molecule containing both a basic amine group (-NH2) and an acidic carboxylic acid group (-COOH).
Do not confuse peptide bonds with ester bonds; proteins have peptide (amide) links, polyesters have ester links.

core.p: The sequence and number of amino acids in a polypeptide chain determine the protein's unique 3D shape and specific biological properties, such as enzyme catalysis or oxygen transport.
bullets: Proteins are polyamides formed by condensation reactions between amino acids.
The backbone contains repeating amide linkages: -CO-NH-.
Different R groups on amino acids cause the chain to fold into complex 3D shapes.
Enzymes are protein catalysts; their shape is critical for binding specific substrates.

callouts.p: The amide bond (-CONH-) linking amino acids in proteins is often called a peptide bond.

core.p: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is a critical natural polymer responsible for encoding genetic instructions used in the development, functioning, growth, and reproduction of all known living organisms.
bullets: DNA is a polynucleotide polymer made of monomer units called nucleotides.
Each nucleotide consists of a phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar, and a nitrogenous base.
There are four bases: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), and Guanine (G).
DNA molecules consist of two polymer strands twisted into a iconic double helix structure.

head: Component of Nucleotide
Role in DNA
rows: Connects sugar molecules in the backbone
Carries genetic code via specific pairing

callouts.p: The monomer unit of DNA, composed of a phosphate group, a sugar molecule, and a nitrogenous base.

core.h: DNA Base Pairing and Double Helix
core.p: The two strands of DNA are held together by intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between complementary base pairs. This precise pairing mechanism ensures accurate copying of genetic information.
bullets: Adenine (A) always pairs specifically with Thymine (T).
Cytosine (C) always pairs specifically with Guanine (G).
Complementary base pairing ensures genetic code is accurately replicated during cell division.
The double helix structure protects the genetic code stored within the sequence of bases.

callouts.p: A pairs with T; C pairs with G. Memorise this base pairing rule for exams.
Be sure to distinguish between the sugar-phosphate backbone (covalent bonds) and base pairing (hydrogen bonds).

core.p: Natural polymers share the characteristic of being high molecular mass molecules made from repeating monomer units, but they differ significantly in their chemical composition, bonding, and biological roles.
bullets: Carbohydrates are made of sugar monomers, providing energy and structure.
Proteins are made of amino acid monomers, serving catalytic and structural functions.
DNA is made of nucleotide monomers, storing and transmitting genetic information.
Proteins and carbohydrates (like starch) are formed via condensation polymerisation.

callouts.p: Learn the monomer and linkage for each natural polymer as exam questions frequently test this exact comparison.

analogy.p: Imagine amino acids are letters of the alphabet. By arranging these 20 different letters in various specific sequences, you can spell out thousands of different 'words' (proteins), each with a totally different meaning and job. Where the analogy breaks down is that letters in words are read sequentially in a 1D line, whereas proteins fold into intricate 3D shapes influenced by chemical interactions between their side chains.

terms.d: A macromolecule formed by linking many monomer units together, occurring naturally in living organisms.
An organic compound of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, including sugars, starch, and cellulose.
A simple sugar monomer, such as glucose or fructose.
A complex carbohydrate polymer formed by condensing many monosaccharide units.
A natural polymer formed from amino acid monomers joined by peptide bonds.
An organic molecule containing both an amine group (-NH2) and a carboxylic acid group (-COOH).
The amide linkage (-CONH-) formed between amino acid monomers in a protein chain.
Deoxyribonucleic acid, a double-helix polymer of nucleotides that encodes genetic information.
The monomer unit of DNA, consisting of a phosphate, sugar, and nitrogenous base.
The specific hydrogen bonding between DNA bases where A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.
Reaction where monomers join to form a polymer with the elimination of a small molecule like water.
The coiled 3D structure formed by two complementary strands of DNA.

mistakes.w: Saying proteins are made from fatty acids.
mistakes.r: Proteins are made from amino acids. Fatty acids and glycerol make lipids (fats).

mistakes.w: Stating DNA is a protein.
mistakes.r: DNA is a nucleic acid (polynucleotide), completely distinct from proteins.

mistakes.w: Writing that starch and cellulose are made of different monomers.
mistakes.r: Both are polymers made entirely of glucose monomers; they differ in how the glucose units are bonded.

mistakes.w: Confusing peptide bonds with ester bonds.
mistakes.r: Proteins have peptide (amide) bonds; polyesters have ester bonds.

mistakes.w: Saying glucose is a polymer.
mistakes.r: Glucose is a monosaccharide monomer; starch and cellulose are the polymers.

mistakes.w: Forgetting that water is released during condensation polymerisation.
mistakes.r: Condensation polymerisation always eliminates a small molecule, typically water.

mistakes.w: Mixing up DNA base pairs (e.g. A pairs with C).
mistakes.r: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G.

exam.q: Name the monomer units from which proteins are formed.
model: Amino acids
exam.tip: One mark questions require exact scientific terminology; do not just write 'acids'.

exam.q: Describe the difference in bonding between starch and cellulose.
model: Both are polymers of glucose monomers
The spatial arrangement of the chemical bonds joining the glucose units is different
exam.tip: Mention both the common monomer and the structural difference.

exam.q: Explain how amino acids form a protein polymer chain.
model: Amino acids react together via condensation polymerisation
An amine group of one amino acid reacts with a carboxylic acid group of another
A peptide bond (amide linkage) is formed between them
A molecule of water is eliminated for every bond formed
exam.tip: Clearly link functional groups, bond name, and small molecule eliminated.

exam.q: State the names of the four nitrogenous bases found in DNA.
model: Adenine and Thymine
Cytosine and Guanine
exam.tip: Can also accept capital letters A, T, C, G if clearly stated.

exam.q: Describe the structure of DNA and how the strands are held together.
model: DNA is a double helix structure
It consists of two polymer strands made of nucleotide monomers
The strands are held together by bonds between bases
Using complementary base pairing (A with T, C with G)
exam.tip: Ensure you mention both the double helix shape and hydrogen bonding/base pairing.

exam.q: Explain why starch can be digested by humans, but cellulose cannot.
model: Human digestive enzymes can break down the specific bonds found in starch
Human enzymes do not fit the different bond arrangement found in cellulose
exam.tip: Relate enzyme specificity to the different bonding arrangements in polysaccharides.

exam.q: Give the name of the linkage found in proteins.
model: Peptide bond (or amide bond)
exam.tip: Either peptide or amide is accepted on OCR mark schemes.

exam.q: State what is released when monosaccharides form a polysaccharide.
model: Water (or H2O)
exam.tip: Standard characteristic of condensation reactions.

exam.q: Compare carbohydrates and proteins in terms of their monomer units.
model: Carbohydrates have monosaccharide (sugar) monomers
Proteins have amino acid monomers
exam.tip: Keep comparisons direct and clear for both substances.

worked.q: A protein polypeptide chain is formed from 150 amino acid monomers joined together in a condensation polymerisation reaction. State how many water molecules are produced in this process.
steps: Identify the type of reaction: condensation polymerisation forms bonds between monomers.
Recognise the relationship between monomers and small molecules eliminated: each time two monomers join, one water molecule is released.
Calculate the number of bonds: for n monomers in a straight chain, there are (n - 1) bonds formed.
Apply numbers: 150 monomers - 1 = 149 bonds formed.

worked.q: Identify the functional groups present in an amino acid molecule that allow it to undergo condensation polymerisation to form proteins.
steps: Recall the general structure of a naturally occurring amino acid.
Identify the acidic functional group: carboxylic acid group (-COOH).
Identify the basic functional group: amine group (-NH2).
Explain that these two different functional groups react with each other to form an amide (peptide) bond.
worked.ans: Amine group (-NH2) and Carboxylic acid group (-COOH).
